catalog_quote: Vowel length is contrastive in Anejom and the Tanna languages, though this contrast is found more frequently in the final syllable than anywhere else. [p. 8] ... Primary stress is invariably on the penultimate syllable in Erromango. In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable. [p. 9] ... it does not match the facts of the daughter languages, all of which have regular penultimate stress, irrespective of whether the final syllable was open or closed. The exceptions to this general statement are not relevant to the issue under discussion. Long vowels in final syllables attract stress, and there are a couple of restricted environments in some SV languages which require antepenultimate stress; however, there is nothing in the phonologies of modern SV languages parallelling the proposed final stress in words ending in closed syllables. [p. 117]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; a long vowel in the final syllable attracts stress to the final syllable; a few very restricted contexts (not specified for North Tanna) give antepenultimate stress. Statement is made for 'the Tanna languages' as a group (North Tanna, Whitesands, Lenakel, Southwest Tanna, Kwamera), with North Tanna data from Lynch's own field notes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress normally two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable (alternating leftward).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final-syllable vowel is long (vowel length is contrastive, mostly in final syllables); antepenultimate stress 'in certain very restricted contexts' (not enumerated); p. 137 notes Lenakel (not North Tanna) shows 'compensatory lengthening/irregular final stress' in a loan. No North Tanna-specific exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a comparative-historical monograph's synchronic overview of the Southern Vanuatu languages; covers the five Tanna languages collectively rather than North Tanna alone; no North Tanna examples with stress marked are given.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is for 'the Tanna languages' collectively (North Tanna nort2847, Whitesands whit1245, Lenakel lena1238, Southwest Tanna sout2869, Kwamera kwam1252), not a North Tanna-only section; Lynch's North Tanna data come from his own notes on one dialect (the one with prenasalised stops), while 'some dialects of North Tanna (see e.g. Blaymires 1995)' have the Lenakel-type inventory (Lynch 2001: 7). Lynch & Crowley 2001: 125 note the boundaries between North Tanna, Lenakel and Whitesands are 'fuzzy' and may form a continuum. Sverredal 2018 is based on the North Tanna New Testament (Carlson translation) and is silent on stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. The book is a comparative lexicon with no phonology or suprasegmental section for any Tanna language; the word 'stress' occurs exactly once, in a remark about Lenakel and Whitesands orthographies assuming [a] reduces to [ə] when unstressed. The only North Tanna stress evidence is transcriptional: the six North Tanna forms in Table 3.1 carry IPA stress marks, and in every one the primary stress sits on the penultimate syllable ([nɨˈpɨtən], [nɨˈpwətən], [eˈmɨtəp], [eˈmətəp], [ˈəlis]); the reduplicated [ˈalisˈalis] shows stress on the penult of each reduplicant, i.e. two stressed syllables in the word. The lexicon entries themselves (Section B) are in practical orthography without stress marks.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The one reduplicated North Tanna form [ˈalisˈalis] 'whip' is transcribed with a primary mark on each half; the book does not distinguish primary from secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The unstressed [a] > [ə] remark is made for Lenakel and Whitesands orthographic practice, not for North Tanna, and the author argues the three central vowels are in fact contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Nehrbass's North Tanna data come from Greg Carlson's SIL dictionary work (1991-2007), elicited at Lomakaun village (Table 1.1, p. 4); the book treats North Tanna as one of the five major languages of Tanna and does not distinguish North Tanna dialects. The unstressed-vowel remark on p. 25 concerns Lenakel and Whitesands orthographies, not North Tanna.

new_statements.quote: The languages I am concerned with here are spoken on the islands of Erromango, Tanna, and Aneityum in the south of Vanuatu. In all of these modern languages, primary stress occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable. However, it is final in the languages of Tanna and Aneityum if that syllable contains a surface long vowel (orthographically and underlyingly a geminate cluster), though not if it contains a rising or falling diphthong. In particular—and this is relevant to the later discussion—whether the final syllable is open or closed has no effect on the placement of stress. Examples from Sye were given in (2) above. Below are similar examples from Lenakel, one of the Tanna languages, and Anejom̃, the only language of Aneityum.
new_statements.citation: Lynch, John (2000). Reconstructing Proto-Oceanic Stress. Oceanic Linguistics 39(1): 53–82.
new_statements.locator: §4.1 'Proto-Southern Vanuatu', printed p. 67 (p. 15), second paragraph; supporting: §3.1 printed p. 59 (p. 7) with fn. 6; Lenakel/Anejom examples (22)-(23) printed p. 68 (p. 16); p. 69 (p. 17) on the modern system; p. 58 (p. 6) on secondary stress being ignored
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 30 pages, no text (extracted text of p. 15 returns 1 byte). I rendered p. 15 (printed p. 67) to an image and read it: the quoted paragraph is there word for word, second paragraph of §4.1 'Proto-Southern Vanuatu', ending '.. and Anejom̃, the only language of Aneityum.' the compiler quoted the printed forms; the existing.lines 806-815) has scanned slips 'Ancityum' and 'Anejom' where the page prints 'Aneityum' and 'Anejom̃'. Supporting passages confirmed in the scanned text: §3.1 printed p. 59 (the scanned text) 'primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable.. stress is penultimate irrespective of whether the final syllable is open or closed' with 'as well as all Southern Vanuatu languages…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Lynch 2001 statement (penultimate, final if the final vowel is long) and compatible with the catalog's weight-hedged penult record; adds that closed final syllables and final diphthongs do not attract stress, that the long vowel is underlyingly a geminate cluster, and that Lynch himself classes the Southern Vanuatu languages as regular penultimate-stress languages once codas are set aside. Silent on the antepenultimate contexts and on secondary stress that Lynch 2001 mentions. The statement is about 'the languages of Tanna' collectively, illustrated from Lenakel; North Tanna is covered only by that generalization.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For all modern Southern Vanuatu languages (Erromango, Tanna, Aneityum) primary stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable; in the Tanna languages and Anejom it shifts to the final syllable only when that syllable contains a surface long vowel (underlying geminate), not when it contains a diphthong, and a closed final syllable never attracts stress. Lynch also files 'all Southern Vanuatu languages' under 'regular penultimate-syllable stress' (§3.1 p. 59), and says the modern system 'can be viewed either as being assigned on the basis of syllabic trochees, or else as being moraic with the final consonant either being weightless or extrametrical' (p. 69). So: penult by default, final long vowel overrides; only vowel length counts as weight.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated: 'I will generally ignore secondary stress throughout this paper, and will deal almost exclusively with word-level stress' (p. 58). Derivation (25) p. 69 assumes a secondary stress two syllables before the primary in Pre-Proto-Southern Vanuatu, not stated for the modern languages.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final syllable has a long vowel (Lenakel ka'paas 'axe', nau'niin 'end'; CV:# finals 'rare — solely in interjections?'); diphthongs in the final syllable do not attract stress ('nakau 'rib', sa'toa 'store'); codas irrelevant ('netak 'sorcery', ar'kanpus 'to shade'). No mention of the antepenultimate contexts that Lynch 2001 notes. All examples are Lenakel, Anejom, Sye and Kwamera; no North Tanna forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Lynch 2000 never names North Tanna. Its statement is about 'the languages of Tanna' (with Anejom and Sye), and its data are Lenakel (exx. 22-27), Anejom, Sye and Kwamera (ex. 32). It applies to North Tanna only by Lynch's generalization over the Tanna languages, exactly as the Lynch 2001 statement already in the catalog does. No dialect of North Tanna is distinguished.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement of substance. Lynch 2000 (p. 67) and Lynch 2001 (p. 9, already in existing_statements) give the same rule for the Tanna languages: penultimate primary stress, final when the final syllable has a long vowel; Lynch 2001 adds antepenultimate stress in restricted contexts and a secondary stress two syllables before the primary, which Lynch 2000 neither confirms nor denies (it deliberately ignores secondary stress). Nehrbass 2012's six IPA-marked North Tanna forms (all penultimate) are consistent. The only tension is one of classification inside Lynch 2000 itself: §3.1 (p. 59) lists all Southern Vanuatu languages under 'regular penultimate-syllable stress' (because codas do not count), while §4.1 (p. 67) states the long-vowel override for Tanna and Aneityum; both are the same facts, so the choice between 'fixed: penultimate syllable with a length exception' and 'weight-sensitive (vowel length only)' is a labelling decision, which the catalog's existing 'weight-hedged' kind already reflects.
